Article Title: As Intel’s CPU market share falls to 31-year low in the market that analysts call 'ugliest segment'
Article Text:
Market share of Intel and AMD in various sub-segments now stands as follows:

How the 'ugliest' segment of the market fared

Intel’s share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. According to a report by Mercury Research, first quoted by CRN, the Intel numbers mark a 31-year low for the semiconductor giant, even as AI spending fueled historic growth for its data center business. Dean McCarron, president of Prescott, Arizona-based CPU-tracking company Mercury Research, confirmed the point about Intel’s 31-year low to CRN in an email following the release of his second-quarter CPU market share report comparing Intel and AMD.Asked to comment, an Intel spokesperson referred CRN to record year-over-year sales growth for its Data Center Group and momentum in its client business unit touted in its latest earnings report as well as a growing number of long-term supply agreements.As per the Mercury report, Intel’s overall x86 CPU market share fell 6.5 points year over year and dropped by under 1 point sequentially to 69.3 percent as AMD’s position grew just as much to 30.7 percent, a new record for the rival, the researcher said.* Desktop CPU: Intel at 65.1 percent vs. AMD at 34.9 percent* Laptop: Intel at 71.1 percent vs. AMD at 28.9 percentThese figures were based on total CPU shipments for PCs and servers, not including semicustom, embedded and IoT products.If those latter three segments were included, Intel’s share for the second quarter would stand at 65.9 percent, down 4.6 points year over year and down 1.5 points sequentially, against AMD’s 34.1 percent, according to Mercury.One thing that is said to have helped AMD was "better than expected" shipments of the company’s system-on-chips for gaming consoles. Unlike AMD, Intel does not have a big console business for its chips.Coming back, in the PC market, AMD’s share grew by 6.4 percent year-over-year to a record 30.3 percent against Intel’s 69.7 percent. What also needs to be noted here is that total desktop PC shipments declined by 20 percent year-over-year in the second quarter.Overall, the report describes the desktop X86 CPU market as "ugly." Hit by limited availability of graphics cards and high prices of components like motherboards, memory modules, and SSDs, the desktop CPU market was particularly weak in the second quarter and shrunk by over 20% year-on-year (YoY) as well as quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) due to seasonality. According to Mercury Research, both AMD and Intel suffered significant annual shipment declines, but AMD all in all held up better.
Article Summary: Intel’s share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. The Intel numbers mark a 31-year low for the semiconductor giant, even as AI spending fueled historic growth for its data center business.

Article Title: Read petition filed against Spacex, after xAI data centers reportedly pushed out a family that owned 2-acre property in Mississippi for over 100 years
Article Text:
Representative Image

Here's the petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant

For generations, a two-acre plot of land along the Mississippi–Tennessee state line served as both sanctuary and survival for Krystal Polk’s family. They raised chickens and pigs, harvested onions and herbs, and traded homegrown peaches for pears. But after what is reported to be decades of weathering racial hostility and hardship to keep the property in the family, an unrelenting industrial hum has finally forced them out, according to a report by CBS News. "We lived a very simplistic life," Polk, 52, told CBS News.The history of the Southaven homestead was anything but simple. Polk explained that her ancestors acquired the land "before people of color were allowed to have land." When her parents first moved onto the property decades ago, they found the letters "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill. Through generations of systemic barriers and intimidation, the family held firm.Their way of life unraveled about a year ago with the sudden arrival of a noisy new neighbor directly across the street: a massive power plant installed to run Elon Musk’s nearby artificial intelligence data centers in the Memphis area.The facility’s constant noise drove the family away from their longtime home. Today, the property sits largely abandoned, overshadowed by the persistent mechanical drone.The site is part of a broader infrastructure buildout powering Elon Musk's data operations, which has ignited fierce pushback from Southaven residents who argue the high-output generators have brought unmanageable noise and air pollution into their residential community.We’re a Mississippi grassroots coalition-turned non-profit raising concerns about xAI. xAI's Southaven power plant, which borders both Horn Lake and Memphis and is intended to provide energy for their data center(s), is surrounded by our homes, churches, parks, and schools.This project has raised serious concerns about transparency and regulatory accountability, and whether the public is truly being heard in decisions that directly affect our health, environment, and quality of life.We have worked to increase transparency— providing accessible information and ensuring our neighbors are not left in the dark as this project continues to move forward at an alarming pace. We are advocating for our communities' rights to clean air, quiet nights, responsible growth, and honest leadership.If you’re frustrated, concerned, or just want to understand what’s really going on— you’re not alone. We believe our communities deserve better. Join us to take action, stay informed, and protect our communities.
Article Summary: Krystal Polk's family has lived on a two-acre plot of land along the Mississippi–Tennessee state line for generations. They raised chickens and pigs, harvested onions and herbs, and traded homegrown peaches for pears. Polk explained that her ancestors acquired the land "before people of color were allowed to have land"

Article Title: Swiggy Dineout launches ‘Order-in-Cinemas’ feature to let moviegoers order food from their seats: Here’s how it will work
Article Text:
How Swiggy Dineout’s Order-in-Cinemas works

Swiggy Dineout partners with cinema PoS providers

“We have recently partnered with Swiggy Dineout for integrating this service into our impact ticketing solution at the cinemas.

It's a very simple and elegant solution and I'm sure this is going to give value to the cinema as well as the viewer and improve their overall movie watching experience. We have already started the integration process, and it will be a very seamless experience for the audience, providing a wider assortment and availability of food on the seat itself.

”

“We have integrated the Swiggy Dineout feature and it's getting a great response. Everyone is loving it- customers are very excited as they can order on Swiggy, and the food will be delivered to their seats directly. Thank you so much Swiggy for this support,”

Swiggy Dineout has launched an ‘Order-in-Cinemas’ feature that lets moviegoers order food from their seats instead of standing in queues at cinema halls. The QR-based feature is being introduced in partnership with Cinepolis and Asian Cinemas, allowing users to scan a code, browse the cinema’s menu, place an order and pay through the Swiggy Dineout app.The feature is currently being rolled out across multiple screens, with Swiggy Dineout also working with PoS aggregator Impact, owned and operated by UFO Moviez, and cinema software provider Showbizz. The company said integration with multiple PoS aggregators is underway.The ordering process follows four steps: Scan, Browse, Order & Pay, and Delivery. Moviegoers can scan a QR code placed inside the cinema hall, open the cinema’s menu through Swiggy Dineout, select their food and pay from their seats. The order is then delivered directly to the customer's seat.For Cinepolis and Asian Cinemas, the Swiggy Dineout app will also show information about upcoming movie releases, trailers, posters, booking links, special screenings, events and promotional offers.The feature also allows cinemas to recommend food and beverage combos and offer additional items to moviegoers through upselling and cross-selling options.Swiggy Dineout has partnered with Impact and Showbizz to connect the ordering system with cinema PoS infrastructure. Impact is owned and operated by UFO Moviez, while Showbizz provides cinema software solutions for PoS aggregation.Rajesh Mishra, Founder and MD of UFO Moviez, said the integration with Swiggy Dineout had already started for the company's Impact ticketing solution.He said:Asian Cinemas has also integrated the feature, according to Jyesth Narang, Executive Director of Asian Cinemas.he notedSwiggy Dineout said the service is also intended to give cinemas another way to generate food and beverage orders while allowing PoS players to integrate the feature into their existing systems.
Article Summary: Swiggy Dineout has launched an ‘Order-in-Cinemas’ feature that lets moviegoers order food from their seats instead of standing in queues at cinema halls. The QR-based feature is being introduced in partnership with Cinepolis and Asian Cinemas, allowing users to scan a code, browse the cinema’s menu, place an order and pay. The ordering process follows four steps: Scan, Browse, Order & Pay, and Delivery.

Article Title: American billionaire Mark Cuban's idea to reduce wealth inequality: Increase the taxes of any company that doesn’t offer its employees...
Article Text:
Mark Cuban wants tax penalty for companies that don’t share

Increasing wealth imbalance

Mark Cuban on how he will use Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini

American billionaire and former Shark Tank judge Mark Cuban with a net worth of more than $10 billion has long being an advocate of ways to reduce wealth inequality. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on the What it Takes podcast, Cuban recalled awarding stock to 330 employees at Broadcast.com before its $5.7 billion sale to Yahoo in 1999, which turned 300 of them into millionaires. He also added that he extended equity and cash bonuses at his first IT consulting firm, MicroSolutions. Cuban argues that sharing company stock aligns employee and founder interests, creating broader prosperity.Taking the idea further, Cuban recently wrote on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) that companies unwilling to share equity should face higher corporate taxes. “Increase the taxes of any company that doesn’t offer equity to every employee on a pro rata basis to non-founder executives. If they get rich from the market, so do they,” he said. While critics warn higher taxes could be passed on to consumers, Cuban countered that entrepreneurs decide their margins and that taxes, even if imperfect, still benefit communities.Federal Reserve data shows the top 0.1% of Americans owned $25 trillion in assets by Q1 2026, compared to $10.75 trillion a decade earlier. The bottom 50% saw assets rise from $1 trillion to $4.27 trillion, but the gap remains vast.Cuban warned that unchecked disparity risks unrest and division, calling it “the most expensive tax on every business.” His proposal comes as AI-driven wealth creation accelerates, with companies like Nvidia minting new billionaires among executives.In related news, recently Mark Cubanoutlined a forward-thinking blueprint for modern healthcare, detailing how he would leverage leading artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini and Grok, if he were operating a private medical practice. The billionaire entrepreneur said that rather than treating generative AI as a replacement for clinical care, Cuban’s concept centers on turning large language models (LLMs) into collaborative assistants that keep patients and doctors continuously aligned between appointments.Under Cuban’s proposed approach, a physician would sit down directly with a patient during a consultation to personally customise their AI assistant of choice. The doctor would embed specific instructions, capabilities and recurring routines tailored to the patient’s individual treatment plan. “If I was a doctor with a private practice, I would offer to sit with the patient and configure their Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok with instructions and skills, along with a series of prompts/tasks that the patient can use and that can be shared with the doctor and inform the patient,” Cuban said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
Article Summary: Mark Cuban wants tax penalty for companies that don’t share equity. Top 0.1% of Americans owned $25 trillion in assets by Q1 2026, compared to $10.75 trillion a decade earlier. The bottom 50% saw assets rise from $1 trillion to $4.27 trillion.

Article Title: World’s largest fully battery-powered plane, X1, completes maiden flight; 30-seat hybrid-electric plane used $5 worth of electricity and other details
Article Text:
Image Courtesy: Popular Science

The flight: 27 minutes on battery power alone

From test flight to commercial ambition

Why it matters: Emissions and economics

The $5 flight

Future of hybrid-electric aviation

X1, the world’s largest fully battery-powered jet has managed to successfully complete its maiden flight in upstate New York. According to a report by Popular Science, built by Los Angeles-based Heart Aerospace, the aircraft consists of 30-seats and it flew for 27 minutes at an altitude of 1,100 feet. The interesting part about the flight is that it was completely powered by batteries. With a wingspan of 106 feet and weighing over 25,000 pounds, the X1 represents a significant milestone in electric aviation. The test flight consisted of only the pilot and there was no passenger present on the plane. Heart Aerospace, the company behind the test revealed that X1 consumed electricity of worth $5 during the entire flight. This underscores the potential cost savings of electric aviation. However, the $5 figure only reflects raw energy costs and exclude other expenses such as crew, airport fees, maintenance, and battery degradation.Along with this, the company also claims that its upcoming hybrid-electric model, the ES-30, could be 40% cheaper to operate than conventional regional aircraft, thanks to reduced fuel and maintenance costs.X1, the electric aircraft is built by a Los Angeles-based company Heart Aerospace. The aircraft spans 106 feet from wingtip to wingtip and stretches 76 feet from nose to tail. The flight weighs more than 25,000 pounds. It comes with seating arrangement for 30 passengers. During the test flight, the plan took off from a regional airport in New York earlier this week and flew for around 27 minutes on battery power. During the flight it claimed the altitude of 1,100 feet. Heart Aerospace founder and CEO Anders Forslund said the flight showed that electric propulsion can now operate at the scale of a commercial airliner, calling it proof of concept for the technology at that size.The X1 flight serves as an early proving ground for Heart's real commercial target: a hybrid-electric aircraft called the ES-30, which the company hopes to bring into passenger service by 2031. That aircraft has already drawn interest from major carriers, including United, Air Canada, and JSX, who are reportedly attracted by the prospect of lower maintenance costs and less exposure to volatile jet fuel prices.Heart Aerospace was originally founded in Gothenburg, Sweden, before officially relocating its headquarters to Los Angeles in April 2025 as part of its push to get the regional hybrid-electric plane certified and flying commercially.It is important to note that electric aviation consists two potential selling points. The first and foremost is environmental: aviation is estimated to account for roughly 2.5 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and planes also emit other heat-trapping pollutants like nitrogen oxides. The industry has set a goal of reaching carbon neutrality by 2050, a target widely seen as unlikely to be met even with advances in sustainable fuel. Electric aircraft, particularly those charged using renewable electricity, could help chip away at that footprint, though not transform the industry outright any time soon.The bigger draw for airlines, though, is cost. Jet fuel prices have been volatile, averaging $3.50 per gallon in the week before the test flight — up 63 percent from a year earlier. Electric motors also have fewer moving parts than jet engines, which in theory means lower maintenance costs, an argument automakers have made for years in pushing electric vehicles. Heart claims that reduced fuel and maintenance costs combined could make its future ES-30 as much as 40 percent cheaper to operate than similarly sized conventional regional aircraft.Heart also touted a headline-grabbing statistic: the X1's test flight reportedly used just $5 worth of electricity. The figure is eye-catching, but it only reflects raw energy costs. It excludes other major operating expenses such as crew, airport fees, routine maintenance, long-term battery degradation, and insurance. Whether airlines would see meaningful net savings from switching to hybrid-electric aircraft — and whether any of those savings would ever reach passengers through lower fares — remains unclear.Forslund argued that electric commercial aircraft could eventually reshape airline economics broadly and help lower the overall cost of air travel, though that outcome is still speculative at this stage.While the X1 demonstrates the feasibility of large-scale electric flight, its range is limited to about 125 miles. Heart’s hybrid-electric ES-30, expected to enter service by 2031, extends that range to 500 miles with a combustion engine range-extender. Airlines including United, Air Canada, and JSX have already expressed interest. Heart Aerospace CEO Anders Forslund said, “Electric commercial aircraft have the potential to fundamentally reshape airline economics and, ultimately, lower the cost of air travel for passengers. ”
Article Summary: X1, the electric aircraft is built by a Los Angeles-based company Heart Aerospace. The aircraft spans 106 feet from wingtip to wingtip and stretches 76 feet from nose to tail. The flight weighs more than 25,000 pounds. It comes with seating arrangement for 30 passengers. Heart also touted a headline-grabbing statistic: the X1's test flight reportedly used just $5 worth of electricity.

Article Title: Xiaomi launches Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 and Air Purifier 4 Compact in India, price starts at Rs 7,999
Article Text:
Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 features

Mijia Smart Air Purifier 4 Compact features

Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 and 4 Compact price in India

Expanding its product range, Xiaomi has launched its first device under smart home and lifestyle sub-brand, Mijia. The company has introduced the Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 and Mijia Smart Air Purifier 4 Compact in India. The two air purifiers are designed for different room sizes and come with air-quality monitoring, app controls and multiple purification modes. The Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 is aimed at larger spaces, while the Air Purifier 4 Compact is designed for bedrooms. Alongside, Xiaomi has also announced the return of the Xiaomi Smart Air Purifier 4 Lite to its India lineup.The Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 is designed for spaces of up to 940 sq. ft., based on two air changes per hour. It has a Particle CADR of 443 m³/h and a Formaldehyde CADR of 218 m³/h.The purifier uses a five-stage PentaClean purification system that combines filtration, activated carbon, UV-C light and Negative Ion technology. Xiaomi says it can help reduce dust, pollen, pet dander, smoke, formaldehyde and other airborne pollutants.It also comes with a colour display that shows PM2.5 and PM1 levels, temperature, humidity and air-quality information.Users can control the purifier through the Xiaomi Home app and use compatible Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant voice controls.For night-time use, the purifier has a Sleep Mode with noise levels of around 32dB(A).The Mijia Smart Air Purifier 4 Compact is designed for rooms that are more than 400 sq. ft in size. It uses a 3-in-1 filtration system that Xiaomi says can capture 99.97% of particles as small as 0.3 microns.It is aimed at smaller spaces such as bedrooms, kids' rooms, study areas and home offices. The purifier also has TÜV Rheinland Allergy Care Certification and is designed to filter common airborne allergens, including pollen and dust.The device comes with a four-colour air-quality indicator and an Auto Mode that adjusts the purification speed based on detected air quality. It also offers Sleep and Manual modes.Weighing 2.2kg, the purifier can be placed on a desk, table or floor. Its Sleep Mode operates at 20dB and turns off the display. Like the larger model, it can also be controlled through the Xiaomi Home app and supports compatible Alexa and Google Assistant controls.The Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 is priced at Rs 19,999, while the Mijia Smart Air Purifier 4 Compact costs Rs 7,999. Xiaomi is also bringing back the Xiaomi Smart Air Purifier 4 Lite at Rs 12,999.All three air purifiers will go on sale in India starting September 2, 2026, through mi.com, Amazon, Flipkart, Blinkit, Xiaomi Retail and Xiaomi Exclusive stores.
Article Summary: Xiaomi has introduced the Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 and 4 Compact in India. The two air purifiers are designed for different room sizes and come with air- quality monitoring, app controls and multiple purification modes. Alongside, Xiaomi has also announced the return of the Xiaomi Smart Air purifier 4 Lite to its India lineup.

Article Title: 10 years, billions of transactions: How UPI changed Indian payments forever
Article Text:
10 years, billions of transactions: How UPI changed Indian payments forever

10 years of UPI : What numbers shows

Almost 13,000-fold surge in transaction volume. Annual transaction volume expanded from 1.78 crore transactions in FY 2016-17 to over 24,162 crore transactions in FY 2025 26

Transaction Value Rises from ₹0.07 lakh crore in FY 2016-17 to around ₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, showing an almost 4,000‑fold Increase

UPI Presently Operational in 11 Countries, Emerges as a Global Platform for Cross-Border Digital Payments

Number of banks live on UPI increase from 44 in FY 2016-17 to 703 in FY 2025-26, enabling UPI's deep geographic reach and financial inclusion

Decade in Numbers: UPI at a glance

Metric Figures Annual Transaction Volume (FY2016-17) 1.78 crore Annual Transaction Volume (FY2025-26) 24,162 crore Transaction Volume CAGR 188% Annual Transaction Value (FY2016-17) ₹0.07 lakh crore Annual Transaction Value (FY2025-26) ₹314 lakh crore Transaction Value CAGR 155% YoY Volume Growth (2025-26) 30% YoY Value Growth (2025-26) 21% Daily Average Transactions (2026) 66 crore Record Monthly Volume (July 2026) 2,366 crore Record Monthly Value (July 2026) ₹29.88 lakh crore Banks Live on UPI (July 2026) 741 banks Banks at Launch (April 2016) 21 banks First Month Transactions (August 2016) 90,000 UPI's Share of India's Digital Payments (FY2025-26) 84% Share of Global Real-Time Payment Volume (2025) 49% of the world Countries Accepting UPI 11 countries

From cash and cards to a simple scan

UPI changed the expectations around payments

India's payments system goes global

Ten years ago, sending money digitally was still not a part of everyday life for many Indians. Today, paying for a cup of tea, splitting a dinner bill, sending money to family or paying for a purchase can take just a few seconds. The Unified Payments Interface, or UPI , has changed not only how India pays but also what people expect from a payment system: it should be instant, simple and available almost everywhere. As UPI completes 10 years, its journey from a new payments platform to a system processing billions of transactions shows how deeply it has become part of daily life in India.The numbers tell the story. According to the Ministry of Finance, UPI's annual transaction volume grew from 1.78 crore transactions in FY 2016-17 to more than 24,162 crore in FY 2025-26. The value of transactions rose from ₹0.07 lakh crore to around ₹314 lakh crore during the same period.UPI witnessed a steady and broad‑based expansion in institutional participation since its launch. The number of banks live on UPI increased from 44 banks in FY 2016-17, the first year of operations, to 703 banks by FY 2025-26. This onboarding covers public sector banks, private banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and cooperative banks, enabling UPI's deep geographic reach, the ministry stated.That is not all. As of 2025, UPI accounted for nearly 49 % percent of the world’s real-time payment transaction volume. UPI has also emerged as a global platform for cross-border digital payments and is currently operational in 11 countries, namely United Arab Emirates, France, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Singapore, Mauritius, Qatar, Cambodia, Greece and Maldives.Some of the major highlights include:But UPI's biggest achievement may be harder to measure. It made digital payments feel less like a separate activity and more like a normal part of everyday life. Before UPI, digital payments existed, but they often involved several steps. People needed bank account details, card information or different wallets depending on where they were making a payment.UPI simplified that experience. It allowed people to send money directly between bank accounts and pay merchants through a common system. A QR code at a small shop could work much like a card machine at a large store.The government's data shows just how common those small payments have become. In FY 2025-26, person-to-merchant transactions accounted for 63% of UPI's total transaction volume. Many of these were routine retail payments, while person-to-person transfers continued to play a major role in moving larger amounts between individuals.The Ministry of Finance also said that 86% of merchant payments on UPI were below ₹500, showing how the platform has become part of daily spending rather than just occasional big-ticket purchases.That may be one of the clearest signs of how UPI changed India. A payment technology succeeds when people stop thinking about the technology itself. For millions of users, scanning a QR code and entering a PIN has simply become routine.UPI did more than move transactions from cash to smartphones. It changed what people expect when they make a payment. Waiting for money to arrive, remembering bank account details or carrying the right amount of cash can now feel inconvenient to many users. A payment is increasingly expected to happen immediately, whether it is between two people or between a customer and a business.This change is visible in the scale UPI has reached. The platform processed an average of 66 crore transactions a day in 2026, according to the PIB release. July 2026 saw a record 2,366 crore transactions in a single month, with a transaction value of ₹29.88 lakh crore.UPI's growth is also being noticed outside India. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has recognised it as the world's largest real-time payment system by transaction volume, according to the PIB release. The government said UPI accounted for nearly 49% of the world's real-time payment transaction volume in 2025.As mentioned before, the platform is currently operational in 11 countries, including the UAE, France, Singapore, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Mauritius, among others. Its international expansion is still much smaller than its domestic presence, but it points to another shift: a payments system built for India is increasingly being used as an example of how large-scale digital payment infrastructure can work.
Article Summary: The Unified Payments Interface, or UPI, has changed not only how India pays but also what people expect from a payment system. As UPI completes 10 years, its journey from a new payments platform to a system processing billions of transactions shows how deeply it has become part of daily life in India. UPI has emerged as a global platform for cross-border digital payments and is currently operational in 11 countries.

Article Title: Nvidia employee charged in Taiwan for smuggling advanced AI hardware into China
Article Text:
How the smuggling operation ran and server interceptions

Accused bypassed internal compliance and false data center claims

In the first documented criminal indictment of an Nvidia employee over unlawful export activities, prosecutors in Taiwan have formally charged a senior manager at the American semiconductor company for his alleged role in smuggling artificial intelligence (AI) hardware into mainland China. The Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office announced charges against nine individuals, including staff from server manufacturer Super Micro Computer, a local distribution partner and various intermediaries.As per news agency Reuters, judicial authorities stated that the conspirators collaborated to pursue massive black-market windfalls – an operation prosecutors emphasised has inflicted serious harm on Taiwan’s standing in the international community. A portion of Nvidia's silicon portfolio and high-performance server architectures are manufactured across Taiwan.Judicial filings identify a Taiwan-based senior manager at Nvidia, referred to by his surname Zhang, as the central mastermind behind an illicit distribution network involving 130 premier B300 server units which, packed with Nvidia's top-tier silicon, is widely utilised across the technology sector to train advanced AI systems.The platform remains under stringent trade restrictions imposed by the US government to curb Chinese access to frontier AI capabilities.Tight trade barriers have fostered a thriving underground market where premium computing hardware commands two to three times standard retail value. Out of the 130 units involved in the operation, prosecutors confirmed that 74 systems reached mainland Chinese buyers, which were either transported directly out of Taiwan or routed via transit hubs in Japan and Indonesia. Taiwanese customs agents intercepted the remaining 56 units before export.Investigators detailed how the defendants coordinated to bypass mandatory end-user verification protocols maintained by both Nvidia and Super Micro, an authorised integrator that packages Nvidia chips into full-scale enterprise servers.The group allegedly submitted deceptive documentation asserting the servers were bound for a domestic Taiwanese data facility, even though the chosen location completely lacked the electrical capacity and network bandwidth needed to run the hardware.Zhang allegedly assisted in securing the hardware quota and attended an on-site evaluation of the purported facility, deliberately hiding that the local purchasing entity had inadequate capital and was receiving funds funneled directly from a Chinese corporation.Prosecutors have requested the maximum legal penalty of five years behind bars for Zhang and three co-defendants, recommending shorter prison terms for the remaining five individuals named in the indictment.Meanwhile, a company spokesperson said that workers are strictly expected to follow all governing trade regulations, adding that the firm is collaborating with Taiwanese authorities to help resolve the legal matter swiftly.
Article Summary: Prosecutors in Taiwan have formally charged a senior manager at the American semiconductor company for his alleged role in smuggling artificial intelligence (AI) hardware. The Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office announced charges against nine individuals, including staff from server manufacturer Super Micro Computer, a local distribution partner and various intermediaries.

Article Title: JP Morgan changed one of its oldest policies for SpaceX IPO, as America's largest bank seeks to win business from the wealth being generated by ...
Article Text:
Chasing the AI and aerospace boom

JPMorgan Chase, the largest financial institution in the US, is easing its restrictions on lending against shares owned by company workers and early backers following recent stock market debuts, aiming to capture business from the immense wealth being generated across the tech sector. According to a report by Financial Times, JPMorgan has historically maintained a rule preventing clients from using stock in newly public firms as loan collateral within the initial 135 days of a listing.Ahead of SpaceX 's high-profile initial public offering ( IPO ) in June, the lender informed internal banking teams that it would permit borrowing against equity in Elon Musk ’s aerospace and artificial intelligence venture well ahead of that timeline, the report said, citing individuals familiar with the decision.JPMorgan generated $75 million in fees for its role in the SpaceX debut. Internal staff anticipate a comparable lending flexibility will apply when Claude creator Anthropic completes its public float, though formal determinations have not been finalised. While federal securities guidelines require broker-dealers involved in a listing to pause for 30 days before issuing loans backed by newly issued equity, JPMorgan's standard 135-day waiting period was notably stricter.Other major institutions, such as Goldman Sachs, rarely delay beyond the standard 30-day requirement before approving equity-backed loans. In an official statement, JPMorgan noted that its formal policies stay intact, explaining that its operational safeguards exceed statutory rules while transactions are evaluated individually by weighing factors like trading liquidity.At the biggest AI companies, top software engineers and researchers often get paid millions in large compensation packages that include big chunks of stock. Lending against shares is a favoured approach for wealthy techies looking to generate liquidity without triggering big capital gains tax bills that come from outright stock sales.When valuing stock collateral, financial institutions need to take into account the volatility of trading and the liquidity in the market, as shares can be volatile after listing and employee shares can be locked-in.Despite these balance-sheet considerations, the wave of tech and AI listings offers advisory opportunities. Competing wealth managers are positioning themselves around Silicon Valley to court employees at firms like OpenAI and Anthropic ahead of public offerings that will mint a new class of tech millionaires.
Article Summary: JPMorgan has traditionally banned lending against shares in newly public firms. But it will now be able to do so ahead of SpaceX and Anthropic's debuts. Lending against shares is favoured by wealthy techies looking to generate liquidity without triggering big capital gains tax bills.

Article Title: In 2018, Elon Musk’s Tesla sent Roadster and ‘Starman’ into Space, 8 years later he reveals reason was ‘failure'; says: We didn't want to ...
Article Text:
“I fully expected this flight to fail. That’s the car that I was driving around LA for three years. And I thought, ‘Well, it’s the first flight of [the] Falcon heavy [rocket].. probably going to fail. We did not want to put something boring on it, like a concrete block, which is extremely boring. So, we went to ‘Starman’ who is flying around, and he is still there. The car is orbiting between Earth and Mars. And we'll be up there, I think, for at least 10 million years,

“Very few people know that the reason we launched my old Tesla Roadster to orbit Earth and Mars is that the probability of failure was very high and we didn’t want to risk anything valuable.”

Inside the interplanetary numbers of the cosmic roadster

Starman and the soundtrack to the stars on ‘Made on Earth’ car

More than eight years after SpaceX first launched its Falcon Heavy rocket on February 6, 2018, Elon Musk has reflected on why he decided to send his personal midnight-cherry Tesla Roadster and a spacesuit-clad mannequin named “Starman” into deep space. Musk explained that as it was the inaugural demonstration mission of the heavy-lift booster, he anticipated that the rocket would likely malfunction and fail. He also said that rather than loading a standard, dull test mass like a slab of concrete, he decided to launch the car with a mannequin.Musk drove the electric sports car around Los Angeles for three years but it is now into an interplanetary orbit between Earth and Mars, where he predicts it will travel for at least 10 million years.” Musk is seen saying in a video shared on X.He then reshared the video, adding:Independent tracking platform Whereisroadster.com, created by Ben Pearson to follow the electric vehicle's journey through deep space, maintains detailed telemetry on its ongoing solar orbit. When the tracker marked 7 years, the Roadster had logged roughly 3.5 trillion miles in space.Moreover, completing a single loop around the sun roughly every 557 days, the sports car has surpassed its original 36,000-mile factory warranty limit by more than 97,002 times. Article Title: China’s AliExpress caught using audio trick to track visitors; discovered after it broke researcher’s headphones
Article Text:
Representative Image

“audio trick”

How AliExpress used browser audio fingerprinting

“The oscillator generates a known waveform,”

“The analyser measures the result after it has passed through the browser’s audio implementation, and the script reads frequency data from it.”

Firefox and Chrome have protections against audio fingerprinting

AliExpress uses multiple browser tracking methods

Chinese retailer AliExpress has been found using anthat can fingerprint visitors by analysing sounds processed by their web browsers. The technique measures inaudible audio signals and was discovered by researcher Matthew Callaghan after visiting the AliExpress website repeatedly caused his phone audio to stop playing through his Bluetooth headphones.According to a report by Ars Technica, Callaghan said the problem occurred because his headphones support multipoint connections, allowing them to connect to his phone and PC at the same time. He had configured them to play audio from his phone unless his PC was producing sound. Each time he opened AliExpress, the phone audio stopped, and it resumed after he closed the tab containing the website.While investigating the issue, Callaghan found two highly obfuscated scripts on the AliExpress homepage. Together, the scripts generated a graph that analysed WebAudio readings from the browser.The system used an oscillator to generate Sawtooth waves, a type of waveform commonly produced by digital audio systems. An analyser then measured the resulting frequency data after the signal passed through the browser's audio implementation.Callaghan wrote.The scripts set the audio gain to zero, meaning the visitor could not hear the signal. The audio graph remained connected to the selected system audio, however, allowing the browser to process the signal before sending the resulting information to AliExpress.The technique can be used for audio fingerprinting because differences in the way browsers and systems process audio can produce identifiable results. Those differences were once large enough to create many distinct signatures when combined with variations in CPUs and other system characteristics.Firefox addressed the technique beginning with version 118, released in 2023. The browser began using its own consistent math libraries rather than relying on operating-system-supplied libraries.Tom Ritter, a Firefox developer who has also volunteered for the Tor Project, said the change reduced the amount of identifying information available from the technique enough to prevent it from working.The technique is also ineffective in Chrome because Google's browser uses its own libraries, according to a Google spokesperson. Safari users are likely protected for the same reason, although Apple did not immediately confirm this.The audio technique is only one of several metrics Callaghan identified in AliExpress' tracking scripts. The other methods he found included:* Canvas rendering and `toDataURL()`* WebGL renderer information, extensions and shader precision* Audio oscillator and analyzer output* Screen and viewport dimensions* Device pixel ratio* Hardware concurrency and device memory* Installed browser plugins* Supported audio and video formats* WebRTC behavior* Browser performance timing* Mouse, touch, focus and scroll events* Device motion and orientation* Properties commonly associated with browser automationTogether, these measurements can provide information about a visitor's browser and device. Callaghan said the WebAudio method appears to be an older fingerprinting technique that may have remained in AliExpress' code despite browser changes that have reduced its effectiveness.
Article Summary: Chinese retailer AliExpress has been found using anthat can fingerprint visitors by analysing sounds processed by their web browsers. The technique measures inaudible audio signals and was discovered by researcher Matthew Callaghan after visiting the AliExpress website repeatedly caused his phone audio to stop playing.

Article Title: US set for largest mass visa revocation in history, here’s what officials say on the visas likely to be hit
Article Text:
US visa

Strict entry rules and increased vetting

Federal authorities under the Trump administration are reportedly organising an immigration enforcement action to cancel the business and travel visas of up to 2,00,000 foreign nationals who have applied for or are actively pursuing asylum within the US. If executed, the initiative would represent the single largest mass cancellation of visas in American history and is said to face significant legal opposition in court.Barring revisions or judicial intervention, the US Department of State plans to reveal the cancellation policy in the coming weeks alongside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), The Associated Press cited internal agency records and confirmation by two American officials.The report says that the measure focuses on B1 (business) and B2 (tourism, family visits, or medical treatment) visas granted between 2016 and 2026 to individuals who subsequently requested asylum. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott confirmed to AP that federal agencies are coordinating to identify nonimmigrant visitors who entered as temporary travelers before seeking permanent asylum status, noting that cancellations will occur continuously on a rolling schedule.US officials speaking on background noted that having a visitor visa cancelled does not immediately trigger rapid deportation; instead, individuals with open asylum petitions will see their legal classification adjusted while permanently losing their temporary business or leisure status, the report noted.The planned revocations follow a string of tighter immigration controls introduced since President Donald Trump began his second term last year, including mandatory disclosures of social media activity, hefty financial bond requirements, and outright travel restrictions targeting nationals from designated countries.Addressing the issue on X on Monday, deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau argued that public sentiment globally and domestically rejects abusive asylum maneuvers, describing the system as an exploited shortcut around regular immigration pathways.Currently, prospective B1 and B2 applicants must explicitly declare they will not file for asylum once inside the country while providing verified documentation demonstrating their intent to return home.
Article Summary: The US Department of State plans to reveal the cancellation policy in the coming weeks alongside the Department of Homeland Security. The measure focuses on B1 (business) and B2 (tourism, family visits, or medical treatment) visas granted between 2016 and 2026 to individuals who subsequently requested asylum.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei: “Intelligence may be very powerful, but it isn't magic fairy dust” - the reality behind AI's rapid progress
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Dario Amodei

“Intelligence may be very powerful, but it isn't magic fairy dust.”

What Dario Amodei means by the quote

Smarter AI could speed progress, but not everything

An AI answer still has to survive the real world

Why physical constraints matter

Who is Dario Amodei

Lessons to learn from today’s quote

Intelligence is powerful, but not enough on its own

Solving a problem is different from implementing the solution

Physical constraints still matter

Faster thinking can accelerate progress

Predictions cannot replace real-world testing

Great ideas still require execution

AI can remove some bottlenecks, not all of them

Technological progress needs people, resources and infrastructure

Ambitious AI expectations should be balanced with realism

Artificial intelligence is often measured by how much intellectual work a machine can handle. It can process information, identify patterns, write code and work through complicated questions in seconds. That naturally raises a bigger question: if AI keeps becoming more intelligent, how much of the world can it actually change? Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has offered a useful caution against assuming that intelligence automatically removes every obstacle. His description of intelligence as powerful but not “magic fairy dust” points to the gap between being able to solve a problem and being able to make the solution happen in the physical world. The distinction is becoming increasingly relevant as expectations around advanced AI continue to grow.The central idea is that intelligence has limits when it meets the physical world. An AI system could potentially identify a promising scientific theory in minutes. It might analyse enormous amounts of existing information and suggest an experiment that researchers had not considered.That could save considerable time. Yet someone would still need to conduct the experiment, use the equipment, collect the results and establish whether the prediction was correct.The same principle applies outside science. A highly capable AI could design a better machine, but designing something is not the same as manufacturing it. A system could identify an efficient way of producing energy, but power plants, materials, land and supply chains would still be required.That is what makes the “magic fairy dust” comparison useful. Amodei is not saying intelligence has little value. He is pointing out that intelligence cannot simply be sprinkled over a problem and expected to remove every constraint. Amodei used the phrase while discussing the potential impact of increasingly capable AI in his essay Machines of Loving Grace. His wider argument considers what could happen if AI systems became capable enough to perform large amounts of intellectual work across science, medicine and technology.A more intelligent system could still have an enormous effect on the pace of progress.Imagine a research team spending months comparing possible approaches to a difficult problem. An advanced AI system might narrow those options much faster, identify weaknesses in existing ideas or suggest promising directions. The researchers could then spend their time testing the strongest possibilities instead of starting from scratch.The distinction matters because some AI predictions treat intellectual capability as though it were the only factor determining how quickly society can change. In reality, many processes have bottlenecks that exist outside a computer.A laboratory experiment takes time. A new factory takes time to build. New infrastructure requires planning and investment. Medical treatments have to pass through testing and regulatory processes. Even when the intellectual problem is solved, the practical work remains.This may be the simplest way to understand Amodei's point. Knowing how something could be done does not necessarily mean being able to do it immediately.Consider drug discovery. An AI system might become very good at predicting which molecules could interact with a particular biological target. That could help scientists focus their attention on fewer candidates. But the molecules still have to be produced and tested. Their effects on living systems need to be understood. Safety cannot be established by a prediction alone.Engineering presents a similar problem. An AI could produce a highly detailed design for a new battery or aircraft component. The design still has to survive the realities of manufacturing, cost, materials and performance testing. Intelligence may remove one obstacle while leaving several others untouched.Much of the discussion around AI happens on screens, where results can appear almost immediately. That can make the physical side of technological progress easy to forget.A computer can generate thousands of designs without needing thousands of factories. But if one of those designs requires a rare material, specialist machinery or a lengthy manufacturing process, the speed of the software does not automatically speed up those parts.This does not mean physical constraints make AI less useful. In some cases, AI could help address them. Better planning might reduce wasted materials. Improved engineering could make manufacturing more efficient. AI-assisted research could help discover alternatives to scarce resources.The point is that these improvements still have to pass through the real world.Dario Amodei is an AI researcher and entrepreneur who co-founded Anthropic, where he serves as chief executive. Before Anthropic, he worked at OpenAI and was involved in research during a period when large language models were developing rapidly.His academic background is in physics and neuroscience, and his career has included work involving machine learning and biological research. That combination of interests is reflected in the way he discusses AI. His arguments frequently look beyond the performance of a model itself and towards what highly capable systems could mean for scientific and technological progress.Anthropic, the company he leads, developed Claude, a family of AI systems used for tasks including writing, coding, analysis and research.
Article Summary: Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, says intelligence is powerful but not'magic fairy dust' He points to the gap between being able to solve a problem and making the solution happen in the physical world. The distinction is becoming increasingly relevant as expectations around advanced AI continue to grow.

Article Title: Scientists got $20 million to build an AI laboratory where robots will run experiments while researchers work remotely
Article Text:
Argonne's Polybot, one of five labs that will run remote experiments for PoLARIS, the $20 million AI-powered robotic laboratory funded by the National Science Foundation. (Photo: Argonne National Laboratory)

An AI-run robotic lab can test materials faster than any human team

The AI is built to plan whole research campaigns, not single experiments

The US National Science Foundation has put $20 million behind a laboratory that most of its users will never walk into. The project, called PoLARIS, will link more than 20 robotic workstations across the University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory into a single cloud-controlled facility. A chemist anywhere in the country will be able to design an experiment, submit it online and collect the data without booking a flight.PoLARIS is short for Polymer Laboratory for AI, Robotics, Informatics, and Standards, and its subject is soft materials: the gels, foams, colloids, polymers and granular matter behind battery components, medical implants and a lot of modern manufacturing. Making them today is slow, expensive and largely done by hand. At full tilt, PoLARIS is expected to run 100 to 300 experiments a day.The grant draws on UChicago's Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering, its computer science department and Argonne. Stations will sit across five facilities, including Argonne's Advanced Photon Source and its Polybot lab, and UChicago's Hyde Park high-throughput polymer lab. The pitch is economic as much as scientific: firmer domestic supply chains for industries worth over $200 billion a year.Co-principal investigator Jie Xu, who co-leads Polybot and holds a joint Argonne appointment, said the aim is to let strong ideas advance even when a campus lacks costly equipment. Access runs to universities, industry, government labs and under-resourced institutions.Ian Foster, co-head of Globus Labs, calls PoLARIS a distributed operating system for scientific discovery, with AI agents deciding when and how experiments run. Computer scientist Yuxin Chen said the system is meant to think like a seasoned experimentalist, sometimes running a test purely to set up a more decisive one later.Foster expects end-to-end autonomous experiments within 18 months. Outside researchers should be able to submit their own projects by the end of the grant's second year, which is when the empty room starts filling up with other people's science.
Article Summary: The project, called PoLARIS, will link more than 20 robotic workstations across the University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory. A chemist anywhere in the country will be able to design an experiment, submit it online and collect the data without booking a flight. Access runs to universities, industry, government labs and under-resourced institutions.

Article Title: Scientists built a tiny 'rainbow on a chip' that could help future 6G networks carry more signals at once
Article Text:
Representative Image. Credit: X (Twitter)

“rainbow on a chip”

“rainbow”

Microcomb could create multiple 6G channels

"The world is becoming increasingly data hungry. We want to send and receive more information, faster and in higher resolution, and millimetre waves could help provide the capacity to do that,"

"They could ultimately contribute to faster, higher capacity 6G networks, but the potential goes far beyond communications. These frequencies could also be used in radar systems as well as spectroscopy and astronomical instruments, helping scientists study materials and make extremely precise measurements of the universe. These applications are still some way off, and there are challenges to overcome before the technology can be used in real-world systems - but our latest work has tackled a major one,”

How the 6G ' rainbow on a chip ' works

"We've essentially created an incredibly precise and stable 'rainbow on a chip', where the loop keeps feeding the light back through the chip, allowing these states to build up efficiently, start on their own and remain stable even when the system is disturbed,"

"It's remarkably robust too. We've even had people jumping up and down next to the system and the microcomb remains stable,”

"Being able to make individual frequencies stronger or weaker gives us much more control over the signals we produce, because different applications will need different combinations of frequencies,"

"Just as importantly, we've shown that the precision of the microcomb carries through to the millimetre waves. That gives us a whole set of highly controlled signals, which is exactly what you need for applications where accuracy and stability matter. That same level of precision is valuable for timing. Precision timing sits at the core of emerging quantum technologies, where extreme accuracy is a requirement,”

Microcomb technology could become smaller

Microcomb could support quantum timing

"We're really excited to see how far we can take the precision and stability of these microcombs, particularly for technologies that rely on extremely accurate timing,"

"We hope this study and our system open up new ways of bringing the extraordinary precision of atomic clocks into more compact technologies for timing, navigation and position, and it is particularly exciting to explore these possibilities through our wider collaborations with the National Physical Laboratory and the UK Hub for Quantum Enabled Position, Navigation and Timing,”

Scientists at Loughborough University and an international research team have built a tinythat can generate multiple precisely spaced frequencies of light at the same time. The microchip-based system could eventually help future 6G networks carry more signals simultaneously by converting the optical frequencies into millimetre waves.Thecomparison comes from the way a microcomb produces many different frequencies of light. Unlike a visible rainbow, where the colours blend, the frequencies in a microcomb are separated and precisely spaced like the teeth of a comb. The light produced by the system is invisible to the human eye.The researchers demonstrated a system that produces a series of stable, precisely spaced optical frequencies that can be converted into high-frequency electromagnetic signals known as millimetre waves.Millimetre waves are being studied for future communications because they can provide more bandwidth for transmitting data. Producing these signals with the precision and stability required for advanced systems, however, remains a challenge.said Dr Luke Peters of Loughborough University's Emergent Photonics Research Centre.Peters said.Microcombs generate a set of optical frequencies using a device called a microresonator, a small structure built onto a chip that traps light and allows it to circulate. An antenna can then convert those optical frequencies into millimetre waves.Previous research showed that microcombs could generate a single precise millimetre-wave frequency. Producing several frequencies at once could allow each one to be used as a separate channel for transmitting information, but doing so requires the optical frequencies to remain stable and maintain high signal quality.The researchers, whose findings have been published in Nature Communications, developed a system that generates several precisely spaced millimetre-wave frequencies simultaneously.Instead of relying only on a laser and microresonator, the researchers connected the chip-based microresonator to a larger loop of optical fiber. Laser light continuously travels through both components, allowing the required optical states to form and remain stable.Dr Peters said.he added.The researchers also demonstrated control over individual frequencies within the microcomb. They could increase or decrease the strength of particular frequencies while maintaining the precision and stability of the optical signal after it was converted into millimetre waves.Dr Peters noted.he highlighted.The central microchip is about the size of a grain of rice, although the complete experimental system currently occupies a tabletop laboratory setup. The researchers are studying ways to reduce its size and energy requirements, with future versions potentially becoming small enough to fit inside a shoebox. The team is also examining whether the technology could be used on satellites, where reducing size, weight and power consumption is important.The researchers are testing how accurately and consistently the microcomb can operate by comparing its performance with precision clocks. The work also includes investigations into possible applications in timing, navigation and positioning through collaborations with the National Physical Laboratory and the UK Hub for Quantum Enabled Position, Navigation and Timing.said Dr Antonio Cutrona, who led the microcomb stability measurements.he added.The researchers say further work is needed before the system can be incorporated into practical communications or quantum technologies. The current study establishes a way to generate and control multiple stable frequencies from a chip-based microcomb while preserving their precision after conversion to millimetre-wave signals.
Article Summary: Scientists at Loughborough University and an international research team have built a tiny microchip that can generate multiple precisely spaced frequencies of light at the same time. The microchip-based system could eventually help future 6G networks carry more signals simultaneously. The frequencies could also be used in radar systems as well as spectroscopy and astronomical instruments.

Article Title: As Disney offers employees early retirement packages, HR sends an email saying: We know that retirement is a deeply personal decision, our goal is to ...
Article Text:
Read the full memo shared by Sonia Coleman sent to staff members ranked “director” or higher

Dear Leaders,

Over the past few years, we’ve made real changes to how we operate, and we’re still in that process. As you heard on our most recent earnings call, we’re focused on meaningfully reducing costs as part of our ongoing transformation, so we can continue to invest in the areas that will drive our future growth: content, technology, and experiences. We’ve been evaluating a range of options, and the next phase includes introducing a Voluntary Early Retirement Offer (VERO) for a defined group of eligible executives.

I wanted you to hear about this directly from me before the program launches. The VERO is a time-limited, company-sponsored program that will give eligible executives the opportunity to retire now with an enhanced retirement package that recognizes their service and contributions. This is one of several actions we’re taking to reshape our organization, including involuntary staff reductions that have already begun in some areas and will continue into next year.

By offering a voluntary retirement program, we hope to give eligible employees an opportunity to make a personal decision on their own terms before broader organizational decisions are finalized.

Eligibility has been determined based on established criteria.* Those who are eligible will receive separate, personalized communication with details about the offer, the election process, important dates, and available resources.

As leaders, you may receive questions from your teams or colleagues once the program is announced. So that every eligible executive gets the same accurate information, we ask that you direct any detailed questions about the offer to your HRBP or the dedicated People & Culture resources that will launch alongside it.

The program is designed around several important principles:

– A voluntary choice — Participation is entirely optional.

No eligible executive is required to elect the offer.

– Recognition of years of service — The enhanced package includes Separation Pay, continued vesting of existing equity awards, healthcare support at active employee rates, and continued Silver Pass access.

– Time to make an informed decision — Eligible executives will have a defined election window, followed by a confirmation period, allowing them to thoughtfully consider what is right for them.

– Dedicated support throughout the process — Comprehensive materials and a dedicated support team will be available to answer questions and help eligible leaders understand the program.

We recognize that retirement from the company is a deeply personal decision. For those who receive this opportunity, our goal is to ensure they have the information, time, and support needed to make the choice that is right for them.

We’re also mindful of what we’re asking of you, as you continue to lead and support your own teams while managing this news. Thank you for your continued leadership as we navigate this next chapter together and for helping ensure this process is handled with the care, respect, and professionalism our people deserve.

Sonia

The Walt Disney Company is extending voluntary early retirement options to senior leadership across its corporate, entertainment and sports units as the entertainment giant intensifies its broader cost-reduction campaign. The initiative, officially called the Voluntary Early Retirement Offer (VERO), was detailed in an internal communication distributed by Disney senior executive vice president and chief people officer Sonia Coleman. The program is designed to allow qualifying leaders to step down while receiving an enhanced departure plan created to honor their years of corporate service.Key benefits for those who accept the early retirement package include a comprehensive benefits suite. There will be separation compensation wherein financial severance pay upon leaving the organisation; Continued vesting timelines for already awarded corporate shares, alongside medical coverage maintained at active employee premium rates. And finally, access to Disney theme parks via the company's Silver Pass program.On an earnings call with analysts this month, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston indicated more layoffs and cost-reduction measures.
Article Summary: The Walt Disney Company is extending voluntary early retirement options to senior leadership across its corporate, entertainment and sports units as the entertainment giant intensifies its broader cost-reduction campaign. The initiative, officially called the Voluntary Early Retirement Offer (VERO), was detailed in an internal communication distributed by Disney senior executive vice president and chief people officer Sonia Coleman.

Ypsilanti Township in Michigan is taking a six-monthin its fight over a proposed data center backed by the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory. Rather than banning the project, the Township Board unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on “major electric utility infrastructure” needed to support new high-energy-demand facilities last week.According to a report by 404 Media, the moratorium is intended to give local authorities time to study the electrical infrastructure required for the proposed $1.2 billion data center, including its potential noise impact and effects on existing power customers. The move is the latest step in the Township’s ongoing dispute with the University of Michigan over the planned facility.The University of Michigan announced last year that it was working with Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL), the US Department of Energy laboratory involved in nuclear weapons research, on a 220,000-square-foot hyperscale data center in Ypsilanti Township.The proposed facility will require new substations because of the amount of electricity needed to operate a data center of its size. The Township's moratorium specifically covers the electrical infrastructure needed for high-energy-demand developments, includingThe six-month pause asks local power authorities to use the period to examine the scale of the infrastructure and its impact on the surrounding area.Earlier this month, the University of Michigan selected a 144-acre site on Textile Road in Ypsilanti Township for the data center. In a statement announcing the location, the university said the facility would have theand said it would not be aduring a war. The university also said the facility would not store hazardous nuclear material and would not be used for weapons production.LANL has previously confirmed that the data center will support nuclear weapons research. Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo told WEMU that selecting the site was abecause, in her view, it did not address residents' concerns about environmental effects.During the moratorium vote earlier this month, the Township Board displayed a stock photograph of an electrical substation behind its members. The image was used to illustrate the scale of the infrastructure expected to be built to support the proposed data center.Township clerk Debbie Swanson said during the meeting.The Township Board has repeatedly raised concerns about communication from the University of Michigan as the data center plans have progressed. Local officials have also supported residents opposing the project.Stumbo said during a Township Board meeting in June.The August moratorium follows an earlier decision by the Board in April to impose a 365-day moratorium on delivering water to data centers. The University of Michigan threatened legal action over that move and described it asThe latest measure does not prohibit the proposed data center itself. Instead, it delays the electrical infrastructure needed to support new high-energy-demand facilities while the Township studies the potential effects of that infrastructure.
